summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing RADIUS authentication clients. It replaces RFC 2618 by deprecating the table limited to IPv4 addresses and adding a new one that supports version-neutral IP addresses, while carrying forward the other objects.

eli5.summary: A RADIUS client is like a doorman asking who may enter. This gives network managers a dashboard to watch the doorman, now working with both old and new style addresses.

subtitle: The SNMP counters a RADIUS client keeps about each authentication server, redone so they work with IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The earlier RADIUS authentication client MIB (RFC 2618) identified each server with an IPv4-only address object, so it could not describe servers reached over IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4668 deprecates the IPv4-only table and adds a new table, radiusAuthServerExtTable, that stores the server address as a version-neutral type plus address pair. The other counters are carried forward, with UNITS and REFERENCE clauses added to some objects.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2618. A managed entity can still support the old table for IPv4-only use or for older management stations, but new implementations that support IPv6 use the new table.

today: RFC 4668 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2618, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. Its server-side companion is RFC 4669.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4668 defines a piece of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing a RADIUS authentication client, as RADIUS is defined in RFC 2865. Management stations read these objects through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

In RADIUS authentication, clients send Access-Requests, and servers reply with Access-Accepts, Access-Rejects and Access-Challenges. Network Access Server (NAS) devices typically implement the client function, so they are the devices expected to implement this MIB. The module is written in the SMIv2 format.
sections.eli5: A RADIUS client is a doorman who asks a server whether a visitor may come in. This document is the list of gauges a manager can read to see how the doorman is doing.

sections.title: Why a New Table Was Needed
sections.content:
The old table from RFC 2618, radiusAuthServerTable, stored each server address in an IpAddress object, which only holds IPv4. RFC 4668 deprecates that table and adds radiusAuthServerExtTable. The new table uses radiusAuthServerInetAddressType, radiusAuthServerInetAddress and radiusAuthClientServerInetPortNumber so that one table can describe servers of any IP version.

The RFC leans on a recommendation in RFC 4001: when revising a MIB with IPv4-specific tables, define new tables with the version-neutral textual conventions, make the new tables current and the old ones deprecated. Keeping parallel tables for each IP version is strongly discouraged.
sections.eli5: The old form only had room for the short, old-style address. The new form has a box saying which kind of address it is and a bigger box to write it in.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module holds two scalars and a table with one row for each RADIUS authentication server with which the client shares a secret. The scalars are radiusAuthClientInvalidServerAddresses, which counts Access-Response packets received from unknown addresses, and radiusAuthClientIdentifier, the client's NAS-Identifier. The identifier is not necessarily the same as sysName in MIB II.

Each row of the new table is indexed by radiusAuthServerExtIndex, a number from 1 to 2147483647. A row holds the server's address type and address, the UDP port the client uses to send requests (the value zero is invalid), a round-trip time, and counters for the traffic with that server.

The counters include Access-Requests (not counting retransmissions), retransmissions, Access-Accepts, Access-Rejects, Access-Challenges, malformed responses, bad authenticators, timeouts, unknown types and other dropped packets. radiusAuthClientExtPendingRequests is a gauge for requests that have neither timed out nor received a response. A final object, radiusAuthClientCounterDiscontinuity, gives the centiseconds since the last discontinuity in the counters, for example after the RADIUS client module is reinitialized.

The RFC also notes that a RADIUS proxy can be both a server to some clients and a client to some servers. An entity that does both is expected to support this client MIB and the server MIB in RFC 4669.
sections.eli5: For every server the doorman talks to, there is one row of tally marks: how many questions asked, how many yes and no answers, how many garbled replies, and how many times nobody answered.

sections.title: Keeping the Deprecated Table
sections.content:
A managed entity MAY keep supporting the deprecated table in two cases: it only supports IPv4 address formats, or it supports both IPv4 and IPv6 and keeps the old table for backwards compatibility with older management stations. The second option SHOULD only be used when the addresses in the new table are IPv4 and can be represented accurately in both tables.

Entities SHOULD NOT create rows in the old table for servers whose address is not IPv4. They also SHOULD NOT return inaccurate addresses or SNMP access errors for the IPv4-only objects in otherwise populated tables. When both tables describe the same server, the row indexes SHOULD be the same so that management applications can correlate the rows.
sections.eli5: You may keep the old form on the desk for people who only know how to read it, as long as you never write a wrong address on it. If a server appears on both forms, give it the same line number on each.

sections.title: Compliance and Groups
sections.content:
The module has two compliance statements. The old one, radiusAuthClientMIBCompliance, is deprecated and covers IPv4-only entities or backwards-compatible use. The current one, radiusAuthClientExtMIBCompliance, is for entities that support IPv6, or IPv4 and IPv6. Its mandatory group is radiusAuthClientExtMIBGroup.

For the new compliance statement, an implementation is only required to support IPv4 and globally unique IPv6 addresses. The address type is limited to ipv4(1) and ipv6(2), and the address size to 4 or 16 octets.
sections.eli5: There is one checklist for the old doorman gauges and one for the new ones. The new checklist only asks for the two common kinds of address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If it is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot change or create its objects through SNMP SET operations.

Some readable objects may still be sensitive. The server address objects could help someone mount an attack on the authentication server, and the client port number objects could help someone impersonate the client toward the server. The RFC says it is important to control even GET access to them and possibly to encrypt the values on the wire.

It RECOMMENDS that implementers consider the SNMPv3 security features, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The gauges can only be read, not changed. But the readings include where the server lives, which a bad guy could use, so only trusted people should be allowed to look.
